EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Androscoggin County averaged 3.13 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.76 inches below normal, marking the 4th driest start to the new year. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).  It was the driest June through March stretch on record, approximately 10.24 inches below normal for that 10 month period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large storm system moved across the Midwest March 15 to the 16th, initially bringing rain and thunderstorms to the area on the morning of the 15th. This storm system intensified rapidly into the evening drawing much colder air into the region. This resulted in widespread snow across the area with strong west with frequent gusts of 40 to 55 MPH.  many area airports reported visibilities as low a half a mile with several of a quarter of a mile or less for several hours. Local news reported that most areas schools were closed and several Department of Transportation districts reported snow covered road  ways. Interstate 80 was closed during the night of March 15 west of Iowa City all the way to the Nebraska/Iowa border.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter snowfall reports ranged from 3.0 inches 2 miles southeast of the Burlington Regional Airport to 3.5 inches 2 miles southwest of Yarmouth.  Wind gusted between 45 to 55 MPH across eastern Iowa combed with snow and blowing snow reducing visibilities between 1/2sm to 1sm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A public weather station at the Hartley Ranch near Roy measured a peak wind gust of 58 mph.

A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.

On March 7, a cold front approaching South Texas interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass already in place across the region, leading to the development of showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. Deep Gulf moisture transported northward by a strengthening low-level jet combined with strong upper-level dynamics and steep mid-level lapse rates to create an environment supportive of organized convection. Daytime heating ahead of the front further destabilized the atmosphere, with moderate to strong instability and strong deep-layer shear promoting storm development by late afternoon.||Storms moved into the region between approximately 4 PM and 6 PM, with conditions supportive of severe thunderstorms. The primary severe hazard was large hail, particularly across the Brush Country where lapse rates were steepest and instability was greatest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Loma Alta Co-OP observer estimated hail dime to quarter sized. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm moved through northern Montgomery and northwestern Howard Counties in Maryland during the evening hours of Wednesday March 11, 2026. The bow echo and associated downbursts/thunderstorm wind gusts caused sporadic tree damage from 60-80mph gusts, and created a brief EF-1 tornado, with focused tornadic damage near Cooksville in northwestern Howard County. On March 12, staff from the National Weather Service Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office conducted a ground survey of the storm damage. The survey started near Damascus and extended through northwestern Howard County. There were numerous instances of trees uprooted or snapped, as well as damage resulting from downed trees. Tree fall was generally in the direction of the storm's easterly movement. Ground evidence suggested the thunderstorm produced scattered wind damage along its path from 60 to 80 mph wind gusts. However, as the storm continued east-northeastward, crossing the interchange of I-70 and MD-97, damage was observed 300 yards southwest of Old Frederick Road, crossing Old Frederick Road between Forsythe Road and Underwood Road. Here, along a treeline to the southwest of Old Frederick Road, approximately 50 trees were uprooted or snapped across an approximately 100 yard wide swath. Several of the uprooted trees fell at right angles to each other. Additional trees were snapped or uprooted near residences to the northeast of the road. The tornado appeared to have briefly lifted before touching down a final time at a residence on Underwood Road, where several trees were uprooted and snapped in multiple directions. This damage is indicative of a low-end EF-1 tornado. Additional to the ground survey, Doppler radar information from KLWX (Sterling VA radar) and TBWI (FAA BWI radar) was analyzed. Radar showed a powerful storm with broad rotation aloft along its path. From radar analysis coupled with ground observations, it was determined that an EF-1 tornado formed at 7:06pm and lifted at 7:08pm, with estimated winds up to 90 mph, a path length of 0.4 miles, and a maximum width of 100 yards. Special thanks to Howard County Office of Emergency Management for their assistance. Additionally, thanks to the trained spotters, media, and public that sent in reports of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 conditions at the start of the month for much of the county worsened on March 3rd to cover most of the entire county before heavy rains began to trim the D3 back down on the March 17th issuance and weekly afterwards through the end of the month. D3 drought ended on the 24th with D2 drought ending on the 31st. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 6 to 8 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2, D3, and D4 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing moisture into the region with temperatures near freezing at the surface allowed for a wintry mix to begin across central Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of March 3, 2026. A warm nose just above the surface allowed for freezing rain at onset and throughout much of the event outside of portions of northwestern Pennsylvania where snowfall was the predominant precipitation type. Freezing rain accretions were mainly between one-to-two tenths of an inch across the region, allowing for slick conditions. Incidents in Clearfield, Clinton, and Lancaster counties produced multiple injuries during the morning hours of March 3rd before precipitation began to taper off during the afternoon and evening hours. Incidents in Tioga and York counties were also reported with no injuries reported from these accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix fell across Tioga County during the morning and afternoon of March 3, 2026. The winter weather conditions caused a plow truck to slide off of State Route 414 near Plank Road in Morris Township. Multiple other vehicles were stuck on the roadway due to the icy conditions. No injuries were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure stationed in southern Ontario with a cold front stationed across the Great Lakes and a warm front analyzed across the northern half of New York State allowed for all of central Pennsylvania to have maximum residence timing in the warm sector. Ample low-level and bulk shear in place across the region and lift allowed for numerous showers and thunderstorms to begin forming during the afternoon hours of March 11, 2026. Cloud cover across much of central Pennsylvania did tamper instability to where thunderstorms were slow to push towards severe limits; however, with daytime heating in between breaks in the clouds, instability pushed closer to the 700-1000 J/kg range and allowed for severe thunderstorms south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Multiple instances of tree damage within severe thunderstorms were reported in portions of Cambria, Somerset, Bedford, and Blair counties before a slight decrease in intensity occurred in south-central Pennsylvania where cloud cover remained more persistent. Thunderstorms began to intensify in portions of the Lower Susquehanna Valley, where multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Dauphin and Lebanon counties during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down onto Camp Drive approximately 3 miles southwest of Windber, blocking both lanes of traffic.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter-size on the north side of Galion.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video evidence from an Illinois River barge operator showed a tornado touched down west of the Illinois River about 3 miles north of Sparland at 8:01 PM CDT.  The tornado crossed the Illinois River and tracked eastward, damaging numerous trees north of Lake Wildwood before dissipating just east of IL-89 and south of Sandy Creek at 8:18 PM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced below average precipitation for the month of March, with some of the area receiving as little as 5 to 10 percent of monthly average rainfall amounts. Rainfall amounts ranged from only one quarter to one half inch across portions of Osage and Pawnee Counties, to as much as five to seven inches elsewhere. These dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand further in March. Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across all of Osage, Pawnee, Washington, Nowata, Creek, Tulsa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, Okfuskee, Okmulgee, and McIntosh Counties, and expanded across portions of Craig, Ottawa, Cherokee, Muskogee, Adair, Pittsburg, Sequoyah, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions affected portions of Choctaw, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began near Junction Lane and Ard Trail in far southeastern Lincoln County, crossing Holmesville Road as it moved into far southwestern Lawrence County around Homesville Road. It continued across Woody Road, WS Cothern Road, and MS Highway 44, passing near the center of the Jayess community. It then tracked across Jessie Wallace Road and Latrell Sanders Road before lifting just north of the Walthall County line. Along the path, numerous trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths. Utility poles were leaning or broken with several lines downed. Multiple homes and outbuildings sustained roof and siding damage, and a business received roof damage. A poultry farm southeast of Jayess sustained roof damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 110 mph.

It crossed Holmesville Road and paralleled Verna Road before lifting near Excell Boyd Road. Along the path, countless trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths, multiple outbuildings sustained damage, utility poles were damaged, a mobile home sustained roof and skirting damage, and a site built home sustained minor wind damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure occluded over the Great Lakes on March 16, pushing a strong cold front towards the region. A secondary surface low formed along the cold front across portions of western North Carolina during the afternoon of March 16 before tracking northeast into Virginia during the evening of March 16. Scattered showers and severe storms occurred ahead of and along the cold front with the strongest storms along the front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management relayed that several trees fell down on Shannon Hill Road and in areas in and near Yanceyville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Red Cross disaster program reported a tree blown down on a home on Welcome Drive in Plymouth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of March 7th during a period of record warmth. These storms formed a broken line of loosely organized convection west of the area that afternoon ahead of a cold frontal passage. While some of the storms proved to be severe in Ohio, the threat waned quickly as they progressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia that evening. Strong wind gusts were still associated with storms as they swept through the state, which caused isolated tree damage in Wood, Ritchie, and Upshur Counties. Further deterioration of storms took place on the evening of the 7th due to the loss of daytime heating, bringing the severe threat to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees were blown down around the community of Pullman. One blew down on Hardbarger Road and the other blew down and blocked both lanes at the intersection of Holbrook Road and Ireland Road.

In the midst of record warm temperatures in the region on March 7th, a broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms encroached on southeast Ohio ahead of a cold frontal passage. Storms first ventured in from the southwest into Perry County, followed by additional cells that set forth their own storm damage into the county. This resulted in downed trees in Thornville and Crooksville in addition to quarter size hail. Thunderstorm activity then tracked east of the Ohio River as they weakened during the late afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were blown down in the Crooksville area.

Further deterioration of storms took place on the evening of the 7th due to the loss of daytime heating, bringing the severe threat to an end.

Showers and storms developed ahead of a cold front during the morning of March 11th, with subsequent rounds of scattered activity progressing across the area throughout the day. A few strong to severe storms downed trees in Perry and Morgan Counties during the early afternoon. More storms and moderate to heavy showers then overspread the area as an upper level disturbance steered the front through overnight. Between a half inch and one and a quarter inches of rain fell across southeast Ohio, with heavier precipitation prompting minor flooding of Duck Creek in Washington County and Sunday Creek in Athens County. Impacts primarily included flooding of a few roads, fields, and low-lying areas next to the creeks. Precipitation tapered off from west to east behind the front, coming to an end in southeast Ohio early in the morning of the 12th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Duck Creek at Macksburg rose above a bankfull level of 13 feet on the night of March 11th, then continued to rise to a crest of 14.3 feet on the afternoon of the 12th. The creek then receded back below bankfull level that night. While the creek was out of its banks, flooding occurred at the campground next to the gauge, Broad Street, Main Street, and fields and low-lying areas adjacent to the creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening hours of the 10th, and moved into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 11th. The thunderstorms developed ahead of a dry line to the west and a cold front to the north, as an upper level disturbance moved into the area. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down a tree on Highway 71, southwest of Mountainburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado developed approximately four miles northwest of Bristow, west of South 401st West Avenue and north of West 221st Street South. Moving northeast, it crossed South 401st West Avenue, where it destroyed a single-wide mobile home and an outbuilding. As the tornado continued northeast across Highway 16, it uprooted trees and snapped large limbs. At the intersection of Highway 48 and West 181st Street South, the tornado impacted an industrial site, collapsing overhead doors and removing roof sections from two metal buildings. The tornado maintained a northeast track, breaking additional large tree limbs along South 337th West Avenue, before dissipating north of Highway 66. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 100 to 110 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down near a farm on White Oak River Road in Maysville. The tornado damaged a farm building, causing significant roof damage, the collapse and removal of barn doors, and peeling off siding. Debris was blown downstream into a nearby|field. Within the debris field, a 2x4 was impaled into the ground. The tornado then went on to damage a row of trees before lifting. Within the area of damaged trees, some trees were snapped in half.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drier and warmer than average conditions contributed to worsening drought across southwest Nebraska during March 2026. D2 Severe Drought was introduced early in the month, and deteriorated to D3 Extreme Drought by late March. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about two-tenths of an inch to nothing, with the lowest amounts over Hitchcock county. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from a little over one inch to about nine-tenths of an inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Record warmth, coupled with little to no rainfall in March, led to rapid expansion of drought conditions across all of western and north central Nebraska. By the end of the month, areas of moderate (D1) drought conditions expanded to severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of March. North Platte saw its 3rd warmest, and Valentine had its warmest March on record. Valentine had its 9th driest and North Platte 19th driest March on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions over the western quarter of Deuel County and moderate (D1) drought conditions over the remainder of Deuel County, transitioned to extreme (D3) drought by the end of March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public mPING report of hail measured at 1.25 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cumberland County averaged 3.39 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.57 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 28% in Extreme Drought (D3) and 72% in Severe Drought (D2) and 8% in Moderate Drought (D1). It was the second driest June through March stretch on record, approximately 11 inches below normal for that 10 month period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Total snow and sleet for the event was 13-21 inches, with higest snowfall totals across the northern portion of the county. Storm total at WFO Gaylord, MI, 9 mi SSW of the city of Gaylord, was 13.2 inches, several of which fell as sleet, with less than a tenth of ice accretion overall. On top of regularly scheduled forecasters, three NWS employees -- two forecasters and the Electronics System Analyst -- stayed and slept at the office on the night of the 15th to ensure continuous 24-hour operations during and after the winter storm. The thick, dense snow/sleet pack resulted in significant travel delays on the 16th as crews worked to clear roadways during the day...before additional snow and whiteout conditions resulted in poor travel again on the evening of the 16th.

Wind gusts predominantly peaked over northern and eastern Maine overnight Monday into Tuesday morning. Winds generally 55-60mph over Downeast region, and generally 35-50mph in more inland regions. Plethora of downed trees, primarily in Penobscot, Washington, and Hancock counties. Roughly 3,000 people lost power during this event, most of which were in Hancock county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Southerly winds were generally sustained at 25 to 35 mph with gusts of 55 to 65 mph. A peak wind gust of 61 mph was measured at Winter Harbor. These winds snapped and uprooted numerous trees, which brought down power lines and utility poles, contributing to blocked roads and power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A developing 970 mb low over the north west Gulf of Alaska, sent an occluded front into the panhandle with the associated triple point tracking over the northern inner channels the afternoon and evening of March 6th. This caused winds through the inner channels to increase out of the south, reaching high wind criteria in Skagway until after the low center jumped into the Yukon and weakened. The following day, another low tracked in but was slightly further south and Skagway saw peak gusts just below warning criteria.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Marine Exchange of Alaska observation at the Skagway Ore Dock measured the first high wind gust as winds shifted suddenly out of the south with a peak of 56.4kt (65mph) at 230pm on the 6th. The Skagway Airport ASOS measured a peak gust of 55kt (63mph) at 415pm and the Marine Exchange station at the harbor measured a peak gust of 51.8kt (60mph) at 714pm. High wind gusts continued into the night at the Airport until 1104pm and at the Ore Dock until 123am.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KCVN Airport measured high sustained winds of 40 to 43 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail was reported southeast of McEwen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions at the start of the month ended on the March 10th issuance as a result of heavy rain in the early portions of the month. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 6 to 7 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface low pressure stationed in southern Ontario with a cold front stationed across the Great Lakes and a warm front analyzed across the northern half of New York State allowed for all of central Pennsylvania to have maximum residence timing in the warm sector. Ample low-level and bulk shear in place across the region and lift allowed for numerous showers and thunderstorms to begin forming during the afternoon hours of March 11, 2026. Cloud cover across much of central Pennsylvania did tamper instability to where thunderstorms were slow to push towards severe limits; however, with daytime heating in between breaks in the clouds, instability pushed closer to the 700-1000 J/kg range and allowed for severe thunderstorms south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Multiple instances of tree damage within severe thunderstorms were reported in portions of Cambria, Somerset, Bedford, and Blair counties before a slight decrease in intensity occurred in south-central Pennsylvania where cloud cover remained more persistent. Thunderstorms began to intensify in portions of the Lower Susquehanna Valley, where multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Dauphin and Lebanon counties during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down onto Quarry Road approximately 2 miles south-southwest of Claysburg, blocking both lanes of the roadway.

Cloud cover across much of central Pennsylvania did tamper instability to where thunderstorms were slow to push towards severe limits; however, with daytime heating in between breaks in the clouds, instability pushed closer to the 700-1000 J/kg range and allowed for severe thunderstorms south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Multiple instances of tree damage within severe thunderstorms were reported in portions of Cambria, Somerset, Bedford, and Blair counties before a slight decrease in intensity occurred in south-central Pennsylvania where cloud cover remained more persistent. Thunderstorms began to intensify in portions of the Lower Susquehanna Valley, where multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Dauphin and Lebanon counties during the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm produced a 60 mph wind gust at the Altoona-Blair County Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to penny-size about two-miles northwest of Lexington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front began tracking east from lee of the Appalachians to the Triad region of North Carolina during the late morning and afternoon hours of Monday March Sixteenth. Out ahead of this front, a prefrontal trough developed across the Coastal Plain. With ample moisture, instability, as well as low level and deep layer wind shear noted across North Carolina, scattered shower and thunderstorm activity developed along and out ahead of the prefrontal trough. Given the favorable conditions a few of the thunderstorms became strong in nature producing a mix of waterspouts and strong wind gusts across  the Pamlico, Croatan, Roanoke, and Albemarle sounds and coastal waters north of Ocracoke Inlet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: WeatherFlow site in the Croatan Sound observed a 42 knot wind gust as thunderstorms moved through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down on the far east side of Havana near the Laurel Hill Cemetery at 11:52 PM CDT.  The tornado tracked northeastward, snapping trees and downing numerous power poles along County Road 2130.  A horse barn was partially destroyed and a horse was killed near the intersection of County Road 2200 and County Road 1900 about 1 mile west-northwest of Topeka before the tornado dissipated at 11:58 PM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A handful of 1 to 1.5 inch hail reports were received from near Berwyn and Cicero.

Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced below average precipitation for the month of March, with some of the area receiving as little as 5 to 10 percent of monthly average rainfall amounts. Rainfall amounts ranged from only one quarter to one half inch across portions of Osage and Pawnee Counties, to as much as five to seven inches elsewhere. These dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand further in March. Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across all of Osage, Pawnee, Washington, Nowata, Creek, Tulsa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, Okfuskee, Okmulgee, and McIntosh Counties, and expanded across portions of Craig, Ottawa, Cherokee, Muskogee, Adair, Pittsburg, Sequoyah, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions affected portions of Choctaw, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in mid to late March. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 5500 acres in Adair County, more than 3800 acres in Cherokee County, more than 2300 acres in Latimer County, more than 2100 acres in Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Okfuskee Counties, more than 1100 acres in Mayes County, more than 500 acres in Le Flore County, and more than 450 acres in Sequoyah County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few brief wind gusts of 65 to 71 MPH were recorded at Coleman WYDOT site along Interstate 25.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rare strong and damaging downslope wind event started in the early morning hours of March 12th and continued through March 13th. Intense mountain wave activity was also a contributing factor to widespread wind gusts between 80 to 110 MPH across southeast Wyoming. Numerous reports of tree damage, power outages, and property damage including flipped over sixteen-wheeler tractor trailer trucks were reported to WYDOT and the National Weather Service. Areas of blowing dust also resulted in lower visibility on area roadways, which added to the already difficult travel scenario.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: All reporting observation sites across the northern Snowy Range Foothills measured persistent wind gusts over 58 MPH in a long duration wind event. Peak wind gust of 97 MPH was measured at Cooper Cove, northwest of Laramie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved through the region on March 9, with a broken line of thunderstorms sliding east-southeastward across Central Alabama during the evening hours. These storms produced sporadic instances of wind damage across the northern half of Central Alabama, with the most concentrated area of damage being across Jefferson County. In addition to straight-line wind damage, an EF-0 tornado was confirmed in western Jefferson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service surveyed damage northeast of Haleyville from the Forkville area to the Ashridge community and determined it to be the result of straight-line winds. The most concentrated damage was observed at the intersection of Highway 195 and Little Crooked Rd around 5:35 pm CDT, where several structures were damaged. A furniture business sustained roof damage and had a glass door blown out, an open air hay shed was flipped onto an adjacent outbuilding, and a larger garage sustained roof and siding damage. In addition, a smaller three-car shed collapsed and fell into the larger garage. Just east of this, at least five trees were uprooted across Little Crooked Rd, with roofing tin from the garage blown into the fallen trees. This damage was all within 130 yards, with winds estimated up to 75 mph. No other notable damage was observed except for a few trees down along Jim Brown Rd approximately four miles to the southeast.

The spring green-up further strained hydrological systems, placing new demands on limited water supplies. March (traditionally one of Georgia���s wettest and most active months) was exceptionally dry, deepening existing rainfall deficits. Atlanta, Macon, and Columbus all recorded their driest September-through-March periods in over 100 years.||Monthly rainfall totals across north and central Georgia generally ranged from 1.25 to 4.25 inches (20% to 90% of normal). EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably mild air moved into the region ahead of a strong low pressure system. These conditions, on top of a fairly dry February across western South Dakota allowed a fire to develop northeast of the community of Green Grass and spread rapidly southeast. 991 acres of mostly prairie and pasture were burned in the fire, with a portion of Highway 63 closed due to smoke and the threat of the fire crossing the Highway. ||Winds picked up dramatically with the passage of the low pressure system, with a peak wind gust of 81 mph recorded at the Pierre Regional Airport ASOS. The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 1 mile west northwest of Summit recorded a wind gust as high as 79 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind of 77 mph. Another 23 weather stations would record a peak wind in excess of 70 mph. ||These high winds were responsible for at least one semi being blown off Interstate 29 near Summit, forcing a closure of the southbound lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure area with a cold front attached to it tracked east across the Carolinas during the late morning and afternoon timeframe. Along and and out ahead of the cold front a line of scattered to numerous severe thunderstorms developed and quickly raced east northeast across Eastern NC, producing 60 to 70 mph wind gusts. With ample instability and strong wind shear in place several of the storms interacted with the sea breeze inland from the coast and produced several tornadoes, in addition to severe thunderstorm wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Between 250-1000 Dominion Energy Customers were without power near Roper, NC. The power outages are due to damage from the storms as they moved through the area. The time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed into eastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 6th, ahead of a surface dry line, and moved across the area through the evening hours. The atmosphere had become strongly unstable across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon east of the dry line. This instability, combined with very strong low-level and deep-layer wind shear across the region, resulted in the evolution of several long-lived supercell thunderstorms. These supercells produced eleven tornadoes, a couple of which were strong and damaging, large hail up to quarter size, damaging wind gusts, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed over heavily wooded, inaccessible (by road) terrain, east of N 161st East Avenue, where the KINX WSR-88D detected a tornadic debris signature. The tornado moved east-northeast across the Caney River, and then destroyed a home and damaged several others south of the river. A large recreational vehicle was rolled and severely damaged. Numerous trees were snapped and outbuildings were damaged. The tornado then moved through another area of inaccessible terrain and crossed the Caney River again, and then crossed the S 4090 Road. Large tree limbs and power poles were snapped as it crossed the E 430 Road, and the tornado dissipated north of the E 430 Road. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 125 to 135 mph.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began on the west side of Beggs, directly impacting the Beggs Public Schools campus. The High School and Middle School roof sustained significant damage, and the bus barn also suffered heavy damage to the roof and overhead doors. As it moved northeast, it crossed 15th Street, uprooting and snapping trees. After crossing Happy Camp Road, it destroyed outbuildings and began a brief jog northward, paralleling North 180 Road. This strongest and widest phase of the tornado occurred as it moved east along Grimes Road. One single-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several other single-family residences were heavily damaged with the loss of roofs and windows. Two fatalities and two injuries occurred at one homestead, where a double-wide manufactured home was completely destroyed and several automobiles were moved and tossed 20 to 30 yards. A nearby barn was destroyed and heavy limb loss occurred on large trees. The tornado then continued northeast, crossing Highway 75, where it threw a metal shipping container across the lanes and uprooted trees. The tornado dissipated after crossing North 205 Road, about three miles south of the Tulsa County line. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 135 to 145 mph. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KINX WSR-88D.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an arctic cold front arriving from the northwest, heavy snow showers and embedded snow squalls developed across western Pennsylvania. Low level lapse rates up to 7.5 C/km, a saturated DGZ, and a pressure fall/rise couplet supported convective snow showers dropping visibility to near zero and putting a quick accumulation on area roadways including major interstates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: PennDOT camera on I-80 at Brookville showed less than a quarter mile visibility with a rapid accumulation on roadways in a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

Hot temperatures, very low humidity, gusty southwesterly winds and dry fuels combined to create conditions favorable for fire starts and spread across Oklahoma on the 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Powerline Fire burned 477 acres across far northeastern Hughes County, just west of Dustin. The fire continued to burn into April 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Elevated to near critical fire weather conditions were present on March 5th as southwest winds sustained around 15 to 25 mph and relative humidity values around 15 percent occurred. These conditions, along with continued dry fuels, allowed for a wildfire to occur in Texas County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This fire, named the Unity Corner fire, started from human-related activities during the afternoon hours of March 5th at Mile 20 & Road Q, northwest of Guymon.  It burned 312 acres and was contained within about eight hours with minimal impact to communities and homes.

A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line embedded supercell developed and tracked over north-central Maryland during the late morning into early afternoon hours on Monday, March 16, 2026. This storm was part of a much larger system that brought multiple rounds of severe weather to much of the eastern United States. Rotation was evident within the storm around 2000 to 3000 feet above ground on the KLWX WSR-88D radar, prompting a Tornado Warning as the storm moved from Frederick into Carroll County. The FAA TDWR TBWI showed this rotation quickly strengthen and lower to below 2000 feet just to the southeast of the mid-level mesocyclone being sampled by the KLWX WSR-88D. The tightened lower-level rotation persisted on TBWI for 1 to 2 minutes after the mid-level rotation on KLWX had notably weakened. It was beneath the tightening low-level rotation at around 12:02 PM EDT that the first evidence of tornadic damage was found. Several trees in a weakened state just southeast of the intersection of Hawks Hill Road and Beth Way snapped near the trunk, and fell toward the east, west, and north. The parent storm motion was northeast. The trees that fell were only around 100 feet apart at most, with an undisturbed landscape around it indicating an initially very narrow vortex perhaps no larger than about 25 to 50 yards in width. The tornado then crossed through open fields, lifting the south end of a long irrigation system and rolling it about 100 feet toward the north just east of Winters Church Road. After this, the circulation continued northeastward crossing several more fields and groves of trees, as well as Little Pipe Creek. The next visible and accessible damage was noted as the tornado approached and crossed MD-75 Green Valley Road near the intersection with MD-84 Union Bridge Road. Here, a couple dozen trees fell in opposing directions (southeast, northeast, east, northwest, and north). One large tree toppled onto power lines taking down a power pole and briefly trapping a motorist between the downed wires, pole, and downed trees. Several large pine trees at the intersection had their tops sheared off, falling toward the north, northeast, and east. Two trees on a hill just east of Mill Dale Lane fell toward the north-northwest, likely just outside the circulation but in its inflow as it passed across MD-84 Union Bridge Road. Meanwhile, an outbuilding just to the southwest of MD-75 Green Valley Road suffered a near total roof collapse, with the west-northwest facing walls partially collapsed inward. Similar to the trees off Mill Dale Lane, this outbuilding may have been just outside the tornadic circulation, with the damage a result of inflow winds into the vortex as it passed. It is at this point where the tornado reached its largest and strongest, with an estimated path width of 150 yards and peak winds of 80 mph. Despite the extent of the damage, only about one-third of the trees in its path at this point sustained visible damage, with no other visible damage to other outbuildings or the farmhouse at the nearby farm. A video taken from the Carroll County Emergency Operations Center showed a swiftly rotating lowering, likely the tornado in progress as it approached and crossed the intersection of MD-75 Green Valley Road and MD-84 Union Bridge Road, just northwest of their facility. Although trees in the foreground obstructed the view and could not confirm ground contact, the video was directly coincident with radar and the observed (convergent) damage. A few trees had their tops snapped off just northeast of MD-84 Union Bridge Road, but no visible damage was noted beyond this point. It is possible, based on the rotation signature on TBWI, that the tornado could have persisted for up to another mile over open fields, but the path length in this survey can only confidently conclude a path up to this point, approximately 1.68 miles in length. The National Weather Service Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office thanks Carroll County Office of Emergency Management for their assistance. Additionally, thanks to the trained spotters, media, and public that sent in reports of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Record warmth, coupled with little to no rainfall in March, led to rapid expansion of drought conditions across all of western and north central Nebraska. By the end of the month, areas of moderate (D1) drought conditions expanded to severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of March. North Platte saw its 3rd warmest, and Valentine had its warmest March on record. Valentine had its 9th driest and North Platte 19th driest March on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions deteriorated to severe (D2) drought over most of Lincoln County by the end of March. Over far southern portions of the county severe (D2) drought conditions transitioned to extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of the month. The cooperative observer at Hershey 5 SSE reported 0.31 inches of precipitation in March. This was 0.54 inches below the normal of 0.85 inches. The cooperative observer at Wallace 2W reported 0.12 inches of precipitation for March. This was 0.76 inches below the normal of 0.88 inches. At the North Platte Regional Airport, 0.22 inches of precipitation was reported in March. This was 0.78 inches below the normal of 1.00 inches. The cooperative observer at Brady reported 0.03 inches of precipitation for March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Prolonged lack of rainfall, top five to ten warmest conditions, frequent low humidity, and occasionally gusty winds on both sides of dry fronts allowed Extreme Drought (D3) to worsen to Exceptional Drought (D4) across most of the Brush Country and parts of the Rio Grande Plains (Zapata) by mid March 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Exceptional (D4) Drought would expand to cover all of Jim Hogg County on March 3rd and persist through the end of the month.  Cattle ranchers continued to cull herds due to the lack of sufficient grazing land, which became dusty in many spots.  Water hauling was required to maintain the herds that remained. Unknown was the impact of the drought on any calving.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured at 2.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Somerset County averaged 2.62 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.43 inches below normal. Since June the precipitation deficits grew to over 8 inches. The USDM on March 31st had 78% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 22% in Extreme Drought (D3).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snowfall around 20-30 inches across the county, with a few inches of sleet, and a couple tenths of freezing rain reported, especially across the eastern/southeastern half of the county...upwards of three-tenths of an inch or more of ice accretion reported near the town of Presque Isle. Some county offices and the courthouse were closed through the 17th due to the storm and resultant clean up.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system deepens over Maine on Monday evening, as low approaches from the northwest by Tuesday. Steep pressure gradient over the region and upper-level jet, helps to support strong winds in northern and eastern Maine. Wind gusts predominantly peaked over northern and eastern Maine overnight Monday into Tuesday morning. Winds generally 55-60mph over Downeast region, and generally 35-50mph in more inland regions. Plethora of downed trees, primarily in Penobscot, Washington, and Hancock counties. Roughly 3,000 people lost power during this event, most of which were in Hancock county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Southerly winds were generally sustained at 25 to 35 mph with gusts of 55 to 65 mph. A peak wind gust of 58 mph was measured at Eastport. These winds snapped and uprooted numerous trees, which brought down power lines and utility poles, contributing to blocked roads and power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought continued into March in northern and coastal Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. Frost depth at the beginning of March was roughly 27 inches at the Caribou office on March 9th, persisting to 26 inches on March 16th. Caribou had above average precipitation, but below average snowfall for the month of March. Bangor's climate site recorded below average precipitation and snowfall for March. At the end of February, northern Somerset, northwestern Aroostook, northern Piscataquis, southern Penobscot, and central and coastal Hancock counties, were included in severe drought. The Central Highlands region, eastern and southern Aroostook, far northern Hancock, and Washington counties were in moderate drought. In March, drought conditions remained status quo. No additional dry drinking well reports during March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A lack of adequate precipitation in Northwest Aroostook led to prolonged drying conditions in February. Conditions were Severe Drought (D2) in late February and stayed in Severe Drought to the end of the month. Drought continued into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Critical fire weather conditions due to strong westerly winds and very low humidity were present over the northeastern highlands of NM allowing for the Helen Wildfire to quickly grow to over 1,000 acres. The fire was reported in Mora County on private land just west of Wagon Mound, NM and west of I-25. NM 120 was temporarily closed to allow firefighters safe access to the incident. There have been no reports of damage, fatalities, or injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Helen Wildfire ignited during the afternoon of March 3rd, quickly growing to over 1,000 acres on private land in Mora County west of Wagon Mound, NM. While NM 120 was temporarily closed to allow firefighters access to the wildfire, there were no other reports of damage, fatalities, or injuries. The fire reached a final size of 1,180 acres by March 5th before activity subsided.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: McDuffie County dispatch reported numerous trees and several power lines down throughout the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornadic thunderstorm downed trees and caused roof damage on Tiny Town Road and Allen Road in Clarksville. Damages are a rough damage.

A strong backdoor front moved south and west across eastern New Mexico late March 26th into early March 27th resulting in strong north winds at several locations. The strong northerly winds aided the rapid spread of the Old 66 Wildfire that began just north of I-40 near San Jon, jumping south of the highway. This fire destroyed two structures, but did not cause any injuries or loss of life. The cold front surged through the gaps of the central mountain chain just before sunrise resulting in strong to high east canyon winds across the Tularosa Valley and middle and lower Rio Grande Valley. Mesonet sites across White Sands Missile Range measured wind gusts up to 93 mph. Winds across eastern New Mexico tapered off during the late morning hours while winds across the Tularosa and Rio Grande Valley tapered off during the mid to late evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several extremely remote mesonet stations immediately down wind of mountain gaps across White Sands Missile Range measured high wind gusts up to 93 mph along with high sustained winds up to 55 mph. Peak winds were observed during the mid to late morning hours.
