EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported on the northeast side of El Dorado, via Mping.

The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in the Central community between Horatio and Ben Lomond.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reports trees down at US 190 at Hart Road in Hammond.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The East Fork White River, rising amid moderate flood stage at Shoals, inundated Sprout Springs Road, which swept an elderly man's truck off the road on the 9th, and while the vehicle's passenger was later rescued from a tree vine, search efforts continued for the man through following days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines downed by thunderstorm wind gusts near the intersection of US Highway 50 and State Road 37.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, reaching below 1/2 mile at times, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 25 mph with frequent gusts over 30 mph. The 2-day snowfall estimates ranged from about 6 to 8 inches throughout the county.||The DOT also issued a travel advisory across much of Southern Minnesota on Sunday due to the winter storm conditions, which included the southern portion of the county.

At the surface, a cold front moved from the southern Great Lakes region to the Upper and Middle Ohio Valley during the early afternoon through late evening hours of the 26th as a low moved east-northeastward from southern Quebec to the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Along and ahead of the front, scattered multicell and isolated supercell thunderstorms impacted northern Ohio as the storms persisted generally eastward or southeastward during the late afternoon through mid-evening hours of the 26th, amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE. The storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage and severe hail. Two weak tornadoes occurred; one in Morrow County and the other in Knox County, where mixed layer LCL's were favorably-low and surface-based ESRH was maximized due to southwesterly low-level jet development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter-size about five-miles NNW of Rocky Ridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the mid-to-late evening hours on March 22nd, a strong cold front dropped across the Ohio Valley, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures in addition to isolated strong to severe thunderstorms. During the afternoon hours, temperatures surged to near record levels in the mid-to-upper 80s, though dewpoint temperatures remained in the low-to-mid 50s. As a result, as the front moved into the region, instability remained relatively limited, with 500-1000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE present. The large dewpoint depressions did allow for unseasonably high amounts of downdraft CAPE, and a strong gust front combined with the cold front to produce 45-55 mph winds separate from thunderstorms across southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. Scattered cells did become strong enough to produce near-severe size hail across southern Indiana, with between half inch and quarter size hail reported across Orange, Washington, and Harrison County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter size hail was observed in the eastern part of Orange County, near the Rego community. In French Lick and Paoli, smaller hailstones covered the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and powerlines were reported down across the Jacksonville Heights and Normandy areas. Trees and powerlines were blocking Samaritan Way and Chaffee Rd S. A tree fell on a house along Normandy Blvd causing unknown damage. Time was estimated by radar. Nearby observation sites Cecil Field (KVQQ) measured 47 mph and KNEN near Bryceville measured 52 mph.

Shear values of 40+ knots and instability values of around 1,000 J/kg at the time the trough crossed the area combined for a favorable setup for severe thunderstorms. The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic and complex winter storm moved into western Wisconsin during the late evening hours on March 14th and continued through the morning on March 16th. Along the I-90 corridor, a period of heavy sleet manifested for the morning hours which was accompanied by thunder at times before switching to snow by late morning. North of I-90, a band of heavy snow set up during the morning hours on March 15th resulting in rapid snowfall accumulations with locations receiving upwards of 18 to 26 inches of snow. As the evening approached on March 15th, a secondary round of snow moved into the area with increasing winds leading to localized whiteout conditions at times before the winter storm exited the area towards daybreak. Numerous vehicles were stranded on I-94 as a result of the heavy snow near Osseo, WI.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall begun in Crawford County during the afternoon on March 15th bringing snowfall totals between 5 and 9 inches across the county. The highest snowfall report in the county was 1 mile north-northeast of Gays Mills where 8.5 inches was measured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured at 1.25 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of showers and thunderstorms, with embedded strong-to-severe storms moved across upstate South Carolina through the morning into the early afternoon. Sporadic pockets of damaging wind gusts occurred, including an area of significant damage in Gaffney.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm survey found an area of straight-line wind damage in Gaffney. Damage was first observed within the city limits, where corrugated metal roof panels, wooden joists, and fascia were ripped off the front of a small business along West Frederick Street. The wind also shifted the exterior metal wall of a nearby auto parts store, causing the corner panels to buckle and separate. East of there, a large tree was uprooted next to a house between Marion Avenue and Mill Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought a period of strong winds, along with rain, to eastern New York on March 16-17, 2026. Winds started in the southerly direction before switching to the west behind the cold front. Widespread wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were observed with some localized gusts approaching 60 mph. These winds along with the softer ground due to rain led to numerous reports of downed trees and wires. Approximately 48,000 customers lost power across eastern New York.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 58 mph wind gust was recorded at the Albany International Airport. A tree and pole were downed on New York Route 443 at Tarrytown Road in the Town of New Scotland. A tree fell onto the roof of a home on Milner Avenue. A tree was also downed on Western Avenue. An estimated 2100 people were without power throughout Albany County.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the development of severe (D2) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across Jackson and Ouachita Parishes in North Louisiana by late March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) drought expanded across more of North Louisiana by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent pocket of Exceptional Drought (D4) stubbornly held its ground over portions of Southwest Craighead and Northwest Poinsett counties. Surrounding these areas, Extreme Drought (D3) covered a significant portion of the Delta. While the winter season kept agricultural activity low, the lack of recharge for ponds and groundwater was evident. By late March, as temperatures spiked above normal and dry conditions continued, local officials began eyeing the spring planting season with caution. Burn bans were eventually implemented in several counties across northeast Arkansas as the landscape remained dangerously dry.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 Extreme Drought Conditions continued to spread across the county throughout the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were down on Splunge Road in Greenwood Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While no visibility observations were available within the county, surrounding counties measured several hours of visibility down to a quarter of a mile or less under snow and strong wind gusts. Wind gusts in the county were measured up to 58 mph range with snowfall totals of 3-4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed in advance of a cold front on the morning of March 7th from eastern Oklahoma into western Arkansas. Wind profiles were quite favorable for organized thunderstorms, with moderate deep-layer shear and effective storm-relative helicity near/above 250 m2/s2. Further analysis also indicated a modest increase in MLCAPE overnight into the early morning hours in the pre-frontal warm air regime, as rich low-level moisture was transported into the region from the southwest. This led to some intensification of convection prior to the arrival of the approaching cold front, with one thunderstorm producing a tornado near the Willisville community in southern Nevada County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours on March 7th, a severe thunderstorm produced an EF2 tornado with estimated maximum winds of 125 mph just west of Willisville in Southern Nevada County, Arkansas. This storm also had a history of producing an earlier tornado in East Texas. The first sign of damage from the tornado was seen just south of the intersection of Highway 32 and County Road 9 near a large open field. The tornado brought down multiple large trees before heading northeast through the large open field. On the far northeast corner of the field is where tree damage picked up again, before tracking across Highway 32 just to the west of County Road 17. The more significant damage was found near County Road 122, County Road 17, and County Road 1702, where numerous structures sustained damage. A single wide mobile home was lifted off the rooted foundation and tossed around 100 feet before landing and being completely destroyed. There was one occupant in the residence who walked away from the incident with only minor injuries. It was at this location that the tornado was rated an EF2 with maximum winds of 125 mph. The tornado then went through another grove of trees before crossing County Road 17 just north of County Road 1702 where it destroyed a small garage/storage unit. Damage from this unit was scattered all throughout an open field all the way to County Road 124. It also brought down a number of very large trees as it crossed the road. As the tornado crossed over County Road 124, it appeared to have started to lift, as damage was more sporadic in a wide open field. The adjacent tree line at the end of the field along the path of the tornado had a few trees down, but there was no clear indication that the tornado remained on the ground beyond this point.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system impacted eastern New York on the final day of March of 2026, bringing widespread rainfall and evening thunderstorms as its associated cold front tracked through the region. Over the course of the event, a widespread 0.5 to 1.5 inches of rain fell across eastern New York with locally higher amounts up to nearly 2 inches in some spots. While most resulting thunderstorms were non-severe, one isolated severe storm developed late in the evening which downed multiple trees in Shandaken in Ulster County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local law enforcement reported multiple trees down on Gooding Road near Crump Hill Road and Route 42 in Shandaken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms swept through northeast Kentucky during the predawn hours of March 16th in response to a passing cold front. Downed trees and power lines were observed in Boyd and Lawrence Counties as a result of these stronger storms. Outside of thunderstorms, a period of strong synoptic winds accompanying this disturbance took place. Surface winds picked up in intensity in the wake of the storms and remained elevated into the morning hours of the 16th. The strongest observation of these winds in northeast Kentucky were noted shortly after the round of storms swept through between 4 and 4:30 AM, where Mesonet stations and the AWOS in Ashland recorded winds ranging from 35 to 42 miles per hour. As high pressure built in from the west on the 16th, gradient winds diminished.

Precipitation transitioned from rain to snow on the afternoon of the 16th and prevailed into the next day. One to four inches of snow fell across southeast Ohio as a result, with locally higher amounts noted in Athens County in response to a heavy snow band that laid across the county and into north-central West Virginia. Much quieter weather returned to the area later on March 17th under the guise of building high pressure.

The combination of a passing cold front and a strong jet stream overhead brought high winds to western and central Wyoming for the third time in as many days. The highest winds occurred in the mountains. Mount Coffin in the Salt and Wyoming Range registered a maximum wind gust of 141 mph. Along South Pass in the Wind River Mountains, the maximum gust was 111 mph. The high wind resulted in roads closing to high profile vehicles for several hours, impacting transportation. The passing cold front was accompanied by a period of moderate to heavy snow that further hampered transportation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 73 mph wind gust occurred at the Grass Creek Divide RAWS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The lack of rainfall during winter 2025/2026 resulted in a continuation of drought conditions across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to begin March. D2 (Severe Drought) to D3 (Extreme Drought) was common to start March, with a small area of Exceptional Drought (D4) across the Brush Country.  Additionally, the area saw deepening/expansion of these categories and the month we on. From the last week in February to the first week of March, D4 (Exceptional Drought) increased across 8% of the area from 18% to 26%, and the combination of D2 to D4 increased from 91 to 97% of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Through March 10, D2 (Severe Drought) was present over all of the Kenedy County barrier island with the exception of the extreme northeastern section. D2 conditions would overspread that northeast sliver between March 17 and 23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: As the tornado continued along Rough River Lake, a few branches were broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms extended from Southeast Oklahoma down across Central Texas late in the evening on March 10th and into the early morning on March 11th, with the most organized threat area over Northeast Texas into Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Effective storm-relative helicity ahead of the prominent line of thunderstorms was quite favorable for low-level rotation, and instability was rather strong as well. As a result, severe thunderstorms produced some damaging wind gusts in parts of Deep East Texas during the early morning hours on March 11th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Small softwood tree trunk snapped and downed across FM Road 1818 south of U.S. Highway 69 and west of Zavalla.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in Dierks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management reported trees down along Yokum Rd and I-12 service Rd in Hammond.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The East Fork White River, while cresting in moderate flood stage in southeastern Lawrence County, swept away a truck carrying two people during the overnight early on the 9th.  Both occupants were found submerged in 8 feet of water west of the Tunnelton community near the intersection of Earl Road and Lawrenceport Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts near State Road 45.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibilities were dramatically reduced, reaching below 1/2 mile at times, as heavy snow fell and sustained winds were 15 to 25 mph with frequent gusts over 30 mph. The 2-day snowfall estimates ranged from about 5 to 8 inches throughout the county. Road conditions became dangerous Saturday night and much of Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The nearby Fairbanks ASOS (PAFA) site first reported winter storm conditions at 12:20L on 2/19 and continued through 18:15L on 2/19. Radar data showed frequent snow squalls with wind gusts at or above 35 mph, visibility at or below 1/4 miles, and whiteout conditions between the hours of 14:00L on 2/19 through 17:00L on 2/19. A peak observation was recorded at 14:53L on 2/19 with light snow, blowing snow, mist, 1 miles visibility, and sustained winds at 22 mph gusting to 36 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Storm Survey team determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 105 mph embedded in a line of storms touched down just north of the Ascension/Assumption Parish line shortly after midnight on February 15th. This tornado started by snapping large branches and uprooting a tree on Te Nom Landry Rd and Highway 308 south. It continued moving east-northeast over open fields until reaching the intersection of Highway 3089 and Highway 70. Here, the tornado strengthened to EF-1 intensity where a power pole and tree trunk were snapped. This tornado maintained intensity as it continued moving to the east-northeast where it snapped a series of powerlines off of Baxter Rd on the south side of the CF Industries complex. The tornado then started to intensify to peak intensity as it crossed into St. James Parish while moving through mainly open fields before it hit a series of powerlines in an open field, snapping 4 lines. It maintained strength as it crossed another open field along Badger Rd before snapping another series of powerlines along Highway 18. The tornado appeared to weaken as it continued to move east-northeast across the Mississippi River. When the tornado reached Highway 3125, it partially snapped/bent another powerline. The tornado then moved into the marsh north of Highway 3025 before reaching Highway 61 where it uprooted another tree. The last damage point for this tornado is along I-10 where it snapped more large branches.

A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of 8.1 to 9 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the western edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 25 to 31 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around one-quarter mile. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold upper level trough along with deep moisture and southeasterly winds allowed heavy rainfall to develop over the Koolau mountain range of Oahu, over Kauai, and over windward portions of Maui. On Oahu, the heavy rain developed and remained persistent for several hours, which led to flooding and flash flooding over the eastern and northern portions of the island. Particularly the Koolau Mountain Range was impacted. Portions of Maui and Kauai also experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain began falling over the Koolau mountain range early in the morning and became anchored through most of the day. Widespread flooding occurred over much of the Koolau Mountains and eastern areas of Oahu. The following event summary includes a list of impacts that the flooding caused. A man in Kaneohe reported forty inches of water in his backyard with twenty inches of water in his house along the Keeahala Stream. The Kokokahi Gymnasium was reportedly flooded according to the broadcast media. Flood waters reportedly inundated homes in the neighborhoods bordered by the Likelike and Kamehameha Highways downstream of the Hoomaluhia Botanical Gardens. A business was flooded on Kamehameha Highway at the confluence of Opaeula Stream and Helemano Stream. The Likelike off ramp from the H3 Kaneohe-bound was closed due to flooding, and cars were flooded up to their windows. As a result, residents had to be rescued from their vehicles. A family on Kaneohe Bay Drive reported that rapid flood waters washed away the stairs leading up to their home. According to the City and County of Honolulu, a wastewater spill at the Ahuimanu Preliminary Treatment Facility occurred due to heavy rainfall and resulting inflow and infiltration into the wastewater system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted into the central US with a deformation zone setting up across central Iowa, resulting in a band of heavy snow bisecting the state. Light precipitation fell ahead of the main deformation zone, however dry air and warm temperatures meant this largely fell as rain to start. The main deformation zone set up across Iowa in the afternoon with rain transitioning over to snow and temperatures fell. Heaviest snow fell through the overnight with rates over one inch per hour at times. Snow tapered off quickly through the morning hours. Roads across central Iowa were snow covered with impacts to the morning commute on the 20th, including an accident with injury. Operations were also paused overnight at the Des Moines airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At 10:41 PM MST on February 16th, the Colorado Department of Transportation sensor 139s034 Douglas Pass recorded a gust to 86 mph. Additional gusts recorded at this sensor during the event include a second gust to 86 mph at 1:55 AM MST 2/17, and a gust to 74 at 5:29 AM MST on the 17th. Additional sensors in the zone, all RAWS, recorded gusts from 45 mph to 67 mph during the period of high winds. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received in association with these high winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Sumter County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on November 11, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in late January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 12 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

A coastal low stationed off the Tidewater of Virginia during the morning to afternoon hours of February 22, 2026 allowed for ample moisture influx from the Atlantic with light snow forming across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Light snow was mainly observed throughout the morning and afternoon hours with heavier snow beginning during the late evening hours and throughout the morning hours of February 23rd across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. This heavier snow was due to a combination of bombogenesis of the aforementioned area of low pressure and ample frontogenetic forcing that allowed for a heavy band of snowfall to form across portions of south-central Pennsylvania extending into the Susquehanna Valley. Winds associated with the pressure gradient of the rapidly deepening cyclone allowed for gusty winds, generally in the 30 to 40 mph range, across much of eastern Pennsylvania with highest gusts closer to the Atlantic Coast. Slick conditions and gusty winds from this system allowed for multiple accidents across eastern Pennsylvania, including one that resulted in one injury in Lancaster County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light snow associated with a coastal system began during the early morning hours of February 22, 2026 become heavier during the evening hours and into the morning hours of February 23rd across Adams County. Lingering light snow did occur throughout the day on February 23rd before slowly tapering off during the afternoon hours. Snowfall totals generally ranged between four to six inches from this system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell into power lines and blocked Little Oak Street in Williamson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving low pressure system tracked across the Beaufort Sea, bringing prolonged blizzard conditions to the Eastern Arctic Coast from February 27 through 28. A Winter Storm Watch was issued on February 25 for zones 804 and 805. The system was upgraded to a Blizzard Warning on February 26. This system produced sustained winds and significant blowing snow that reduced visibilities to near zero for over 36 hours. The warning was cancelled on the morning of February 28, as the low pressure center weekend and shifted inland. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two distinct periods of blizzard conditions impacted the area. The first period began at 1500AKST on February 27 and continued through 0020AKST on February 28 at Deadhorse, with Nuiqsut observing blizzard conditions between 1545AKST and 2315AKST on the same date. The second period began at 1640AKST on February 28 and continued through 0530AKST on March 1 at Deadhorse.||During the initial wave, sustained winds of thirty-nine miles per hour with a peak wind gust of fifty-nine miles per hour and visibility less than one-quarter mile were measured by the Deadhorse ASOS (PASC) at 2053AKST on February 27. The second period of blizzard conditions developed at 1640AKST on February 28. This second wave produced sustained winds of forty miles per hour with a peak gust of fifty-six miles per hour with snow and visibility below one-quarter mile at PASC at 2253AKST on February 28.||The Blizzard Warning was downgraded to a Winter Weather Advisory at 0241AKST on February 28 then upgraded to a Blizzard Warning at 1705AKST on the same date.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure developed across the High Plains on the 17th and moved across the Dakotas on the 18th and into northern Wisconsin on the morning of the 19th. This led to a prolonged period of snowfall across the region. The track of this low was favorable for lake and terrain enhancement along the North Shore. Additionally, the strong low led to very gusty winds along the North Shore that led to a prolonged period of blizzard conditions that led to the closure of Minnesota Highway 61 for about 3 hours as crews were unable to keep up with the snowfall. Snowfall accumulations inland of Lake Superior were 6 to 10 inch range with much higher amounts along the North Shore, including upwards of 40 inches for the event in Hovland right on the shore of Lake Superior.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals across the county were in the 3 to 7 inch range. A high amount of 8 inches was reported in the far southeast corner of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month. Central Illinois then experienced one of the driest Februarys on record, and the Severe Drought (D2) persisted through the end of the month. Streamflows and soil moisture values across the region ranged from well below normal to near record lows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blizzard conditions impacted the Baldwin Peninsula, where a Blizzard Warning was in effect from 0431AKST on February 20 through 0843AKST on February 22, 2026. The Ralph Wien Memorial Airport ASOS (PAOT) in Kotzebue reported that blizzard conditions began at 0045AKST on February 21. The third hour of continuous blizzard criteria verified the warning at 0345AKST on February 21. During the peak of the event, PAOT measured visibilities of one-quarter mile in heavy snow, with sustained winds of forty-five miles per hour and a peak gust of sixty miles per hour. Blizzard conditions concluded at 1835AKST on February 21. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Nenana SNOTEL (NESA2) reported a snow depth increase of 9 inches in less than 24 hours from 2/17 at 16:00L to 2/18 at 11:00L. Additionally, an Alaska 511 report at 05:15L on 2/18 reported snowfall totals between 4 to 10 inches along the Parks Highway from MP 276 to MP 316. A peak observation was recorded at the Nenana ASOS site (PANN) at 09:21L on 2/18 with snow, ice fog, 1/4 mile visibility, and sustained winds at 14 mph gusting to 21 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down along August Ln, just west of Polo Rd, where it damaged trees and a roof of a residence. It moved east along Polo Rd with sporadic tree damage. The heaviest tree damage occurred along Spirit of the Forest Ln and River Trace Rd where more than a dozen very large trees were uprooted or snapped. Periodic tree and large limb damage occurred along the remainder of the path until the tornado lifted in the Merrywood Estates subdivision. Path length was 9.3 miles. Max width was 75 yards. Estimated maximum winds around 95 mph.

A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of 5.2 to 8 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the northwestern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 20 to 25 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around one-quarter mile.

The initial burst of winds arrived in the late morning timeframe with the frontal passage, and continued to be breezy to strong through the day as stronger winds from aloft mixed down to the surface. The strongest winds in the area measured that day was reported from an AWOS observation site in the town of Jackson with a 47 mile per hour gust noted around the time of the front's passage. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of top-ten hottest temperatures and virtually no rainfall in February allowed Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought to persist across locations from Hidalgo and Kenedy County west to Zapata County through February.  Coverage of D2 and D3 conditions would steadily expand as the month wore on.  Cattle ranchers began to report culling of herds, dried out rangelands, and the need to haul water on more occasions. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stacked surface low was located over northeastern MN. An area of deformation developed across the Dakotas and moved slowly into Minnesota. Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. Additionally, due to the strength of the pressure gradient, wind gusts across much of western MN ranged between 35 to 50 mph. The rate of falling and blowing snow reduced visibility to whiteout conditions, making many roadways impassible. Snow lingered for several hours before finally dissipating the afternoon of the following day. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic trough pushed through Southcentral Alaska on February 24. A 980 mb surface low formed over the northeastern Gulf of Alaska coast. A strong pressure gradient formed between the coastal low and high pressure over the Bering, which, combined with a strong temperature gradient over and through the mountains, triggered northerly gap winds across the region, including Thompson Pass and Kodiak Island. Thompson Pass saw strong winds, which combined with transportable snow, led to blizzard conditions that lasted through February 26. Kodiak Island saw a period of gusty winds on February 25.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Alaska Department of Transportation (AKDOT) reported on February 24 that winds were gusting up to 60 mph with zero visibility from Paxson Camp to Trims Camp. There was significant drifting of snow that completely obscured the road with the plow operator having to stop at times and make sure that he was still on the road. AKDOT closed Isabel Pass due to ground blizzard conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted into the central US with a deformation zone setting up across central Iowa, resulting in a band of heavy snow bisecting the state. Light precipitation fell ahead of the main deformation zone, however dry air and warm temperatures meant this largely fell as rain to start. The main deformation zone set up across Iowa in the afternoon with rain transitioning over to snow and temperatures fell. Heaviest snow fell through the overnight with rates over one inch per hour at times. Snow tapered off quickly through the morning hours. Roads across central Iowa were snow covered with impacts to the morning commute on the 20th, including an accident with injury. Operations were also paused overnight at the Des Moines airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Eastern Oklahoma experienced only one rainfall event during the month of February. During this mid-month event, rainfall across the region ranged from one hundredth to one tenth of an inch across portions of northeastern Oklahoma to as much as three to four inches across portions of east central and southeastern Oklahoma. The rainfall that fell across eastern Oklahoma in February was below the monthly average amounts for much of the region, with a large portion of northeastern Oklahoma only receiving from one to five percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. These very dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand in February. Severe (D2) drought conditions developed across all of Washington, Nowata, Craig, Ottawa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties, and developed across portions of Tulsa, Muskogee, Adair, McIntosh, Pittsburg, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed into portions of Choctaw, Ottawa, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, Cherokee, Muskogee and Adair Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system developed along a baroclinic zone off the coast of Georgia during the overnight hours between Friday January thirtieth and Saturday January thirty-first. This low then began to rapidly deepen during the evening hours of January thirty-first while tracking northeastwards along the Carolina Coast making its closest point of approach to the coastal waters near North Carolina during the early morning hours of Sunday February first with a minimum pressure around 994 mb before the system departed off to the north and east. With strong high pressure ridging building in from the north and west a tight pressure gradient spread over most of our waters bringing Storm Force wind gusts to much of the coastal and interior waters of eastern North Carolina during the evening of January thirty-first to the morning of February first.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oregon Inlet CG XORE WeatherFlow site measured several hours of frequent storm force wind gusts between the evening of January thirty-first and the morning of February first. Reports came in via WeatherFlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days leading up to this event, a strong trough made landfall along the West Coast of the US. Ahead of this system, unusually warm and dry conditions prevailed as high pressure dominated the Intermountain West. The trough began to track inland on the 15th into the 16th, but the high pressure was reluctant to shift east. This led to a tightening up of the pressure gradient between these two features, enhancing an already strong southwesterly upper level jet. Lift began to increase ahead of the trough on the evening of the 16th, with mountain rain and snow showers breaking out over the higher terrain of eastern Utah and western Colorado. This also helped to keep deep mixing ongoing well after sunset, resulting in some of the peak winds occurring between midnight and daybreak on the 17th. In addition, a potent cold front was associated with this system, and was expected to sweep through eastern Utah and western Colorado around daybreak. Ahead of the cold front, the surface pressure gradient tightened substantially and surface winds maxed out. This coincided with the period between midnight and daybreak on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The peak gust recorded during this event was to 71 mph at the Hallenbeck Reservoir DRI mesonet sensor at 3:15 AM MST 2/17. Gusts at or above 58 mph began as early as 6:45 PM MST 2/16, again with a gust at the Hallenbeck Reservoir site. A gust to 60 mph was recorded at the KGJT ASOS at Grand Junction Regional Airport at 1:33 AM MST 2/17. Additional gusts between 45 mph and 55 mph were recorded across the region during the period of high winds. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received in association with this event.

While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state.
